set.st: On the night of Friday 20 September 1889 nearly $40,000 of express-company money was taken from the vault of the Iron Exchange Bank at Hurley, opened with the combination. It was an inside job: in November 1889 the bank's bookkeeper and an Ironwood saloonkeeper were arrested; the saloonkeeper was convicted at Ashland in June 1890 and served five years at Waupun. The amount was put at $39,000 and only about $1,100 was ever recovered. In July 1890 the bookkeeper's stepfather, a New London banker, was arrested for passing some of the stolen bills; at his trial in Oshkosh in December 1890 the prosecutor said the notes 'appeared to have lain in water or to have been concealed in the earth', and he was convicted on 15 January 1891. An 1898 retrospective put the total at $41,000. No recovery of the rest was ever reported, so part of the cache had been dug up within a year and the remainder was never found. When he was released in April 1895 the Marinette Eagle reported the detectives' belief that the money had been carried to some point north of Hurley and buried, or sunk in a watertight box in the Montreal River; a Duluth paper the same week said buried in Ashland or Iron County or sunk in the river. No find was ever reported.
set.t: Lead grade C: the robbery, conviction, $1,100 recovery and the earth-stained bills at the 1890 trial are period record; where the rest went rests on one 1895 detective theory. The Montreal River north of Hurley is the state line through county forest and private land; look only, and diving or digging needs permission.
set.tovw: Lead grade C: period papers confirm the 1889 theft, that about $37,900 was never recovered, and (at the 1890 trial) that bills from the loot had lain in water or earth; the 1895 detectives' theory agrees on burial or the Montreal River, but no place closer than north of Hurley is given
